title: Does Explicit Instruction Work For Students with Learning Difficulties
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick reviews a computational study from the University of Haifa that compared how adults with ADHD, dyslexia and neurotypical controls learned a complex, multidimensional task with and without explicit guidance about what to attend to. He frames it against a once-dominant belief that students with learning difficulties need more discovery and exploration, and argues the study shows explicit guidance is not just helpful for them but essential. Students with ADHD paid what he calls a 'discovery tax', performing markedly worse without guidance and relying less on optimal Bayesian strategies, while students with dyslexia showed accelerated forgetting that unguided discovery made worse. He draws out the equity implication that discovery-based approaches impose avoidable cognitive burdens on these learners, and argues that explicit instruction, scaffolding and responsive teaching level the cognitive playing field. He is candid about limitations, notably adult participants and small samples, and closes with open questions for practice about balancing guidance, review and challenge.
points: Hendrick reports that ADHD participants performed significantly worse when forced to discover patterns unaided, a 'discovery tax' their neurotypical peers did not pay.
For dyslexic participants the study found heightened decay rates, so unguided discovery was a double penalty: harder to learn initially and harder to remember afterwards.
Computational modelling showed ADHD learners relied more on simple reinforcement learning than Bayesian inference, which he frames as a difference in cognitive architecture, not intelligence.
He argues explicit guidance, modelling and structured practice with feedback do not do the thinking for students but remove barriers to thinking effectively.
He flags the study's adult participants and roughly 20-per-group samples as real limits, raising the risk of Type II errors.
quotes: The final part of that calculus was that if students with learning difficulties are struggling, they simply need more opportunities to explore and construct meaning at their own pace. Often this manifested itself as teaching that was low in expectation and high in sentiment.

The results were clear. Students with ADHD showed significantly worse performance when forced to discover patterns without guidance. They could learn when given explicit direction about what mattered, but struggled markedly when that scaffolding was removed.

Instead, they relied more heavily on simpler reinforcement learning mechanisms. This isn't a deficit in intelligence; it's a difference in cognitive architecture. But it means that when learning environments demand complex strategy selection (as discovery-based approaches inevitably do) these students are operating with fundamentally inadequate tools.

This finding illuminates why discovery approaches often fail these students so dramatically. Not only are they being asked to identify relevant patterns without guidance, but the cognitive effort required to do so actively undermines their ability to retain what they've learned. It's a double penalty: harder to learn initially, and harder to remember afterwards.

This isn't about lowering expectations or "dumbing down" instruction. Students with ADHD and dyslexia in this study learned successfully when provided with appropriate scaffolding. The issue is that unguided discovery asks them to simultaneously master content while managing cognitive processes that their peers handle more automatically.
We're not doing the thinking for students. We're removing the barriers that prevent them from thinking effectively.

As we continue to refine our understanding of learning differences, one thing becomes clear: effective instruction isn't about choosing between explicit and implicit approaches. It's about understanding the cognitive demands of different learning environments and matching instructional support to student needs.
